1:
Chrysostom states the trouble before touching the words. Many Jews had believed and still adhered in conscience to the law; rather than be detected abstaining from swine's flesh alone they gave up all flesh and lived on herbs, so that what they did might look more like a fast than an observance. Others, further advanced, kept none of it, and became offensive to the first by reproaching and accusing them until they were driven to despondency. Paul, he says, feared that a wish to be right about a trifle would overthrow the whole. Theodoret compresses the same judgment into a sentence: by weak the apostle means the man still a slave to legal observances. Henry, whose exposition here opens the chapter as a whole, traces the quarrel to the mixed membership of the Roman church, where what had been bred in the bone could hardly be got out of the flesh even after conversion. Gill allows the phrase two senses, weakness in the grace of faith and weakness in the doctrine of faith, and takes the second, an understanding still a child that cannot bear strong meat.

On the command itself Ellicott takes receive as the stretching out of the hand of friendship, and prefers the margin in the clause that follows, not to judge his doubtful thoughts or criticise his scruples: the strong are to deal tenderly and not draw the weak into casuistical discussion. Robertson agrees that the strong brother is not called on to settle all the scruples of the weak. Wesley reads the scruples as needless and the reception as one of love and courtesy into fellowship.

Barnes takes the second verse to turn on meat offered in sacrifice to idols, part of the animal being burnt and the rest eaten or sold in the market, and refers the reader to the principle he finds settled in the first epistle to Corinth. Clarke explains the practice of the Jew in a heathen country from the same difficulty: not knowing whether what the market sells came from a clean beast, was offered to an idol, or was properly bled, the scrupulous man avoids flesh altogether. Calvin denies that this is the heathen abstinence grounded on the transmigration of souls, since the apostle would not have handled so absurd a notion in this way, and argues from history that Jews living among heathens abstained wholly for fear of contamination. Theodoret reports a harsher account, that the Jewish converts abstained even from all animal food under a pretext of temperance in order to shame the Gentiles.

The third verse divides the fault, and here the voices are unanimous. Barnes calls the two words happily chosen: the Gentile is likely to despise the Jew as foolishly scrupulous, while the Jew, thinking the matter too serious for contempt, assumes the right to condemn. Ellicott puts it that the strong despise the weak and the weak judge the strong, contempt for supposed narrowness meeting censure of supposed levity, and adds that human nature alters very little. Calvin draws the reason out for both parties at once: where you see a man illuminated with the knowledge of God you have evidence enough that God has received him, and if you either despise or condemn him you reject the man God has embraced. Clarke adds that both, being sincere and acting in the fear of God, are received as heirs without difference on account of these scruples.
4:
The argument turns on a case from civil life. Gill and Barnes both take it that one man has no power over another man's servant and no right to call him to account; Barnes adds that to attempt it is to become a busybody in other men's matters. Calvin puts the challenge in the second person and then draws a line the others leave implicit: the power of judging is taken from us as to the man, whom we must leave to God, but not as to the deed, on which we may form a decisive opinion, provided it is drawn from the word of God and so is neither human nor another man's judgment. Theodoret grounds the servant's belonging in the price paid, the Lord of all having bought him with his own blood. On the promise that he shall be holden up, Clarke reads it of the sincere though scrupulous man whom God will uphold, and adds that it is God's will such persons continue members of his Church. Ellicott takes the standing and falling judicially, of acquittal or condemnation by the Master, notes that the true reading names the Lord rather than God, and holds that the trial is not reserved for the last day but is a judgment Christ may pass at any moment. Robertson observes only that the verb is a passive future, he shall be made to stand, in spite of your sharp criticisms of one another.

On the second instance, that of days, Gill labours to exclude every reading but the Jewish one: not the fasts of later Christian appointment, which had not yet been introduced at Rome, and not the lucky and unlucky days of the heathen, since the apostle would not say that a man who regarded such a day regarded it to the Lord. Barnes and Calvin agree that the festivals were designed to keep Israel a separate people and vanished with the Messiah, and Calvin adds that the scruple was itself an evidence of weakness, though acting against conscience would have been presumption. Here the strongest disagreement in the chapter appears. Barnes observes that the word alike is not in the original and may convey a wrong idea; Clarke turns the same observation into a protest, that by adding it we make the text say what was never intended, that there is no distinction of days, not even of the Sabbath, which he holds of lasting obligation. Ellicott, comparing Galatians and Colossians, concludes instead that the observance of special days has no absolute sanction but is a question of religious expediency. Robertson notes the plain historical fact that the Jewish Christians still kept the seventh day while the Gentiles were keeping the first in honour of the Resurrection, and that Paul pleads for liberty; Wesley asks only that a man be persuaded a thing is lawful before he does it.

The reason given is that each acts unto the Lord. Gill and Clarke take this at face value, the one obeying commands he thinks still binding, the other honouring God by not observing what he does not believe enjoined, and both giving thanks. Calvin will not let it pass so easily: the notion behind the day-keeping was superstitious and he does not deny it, but what God approved was that the man dared not act with a doubtful conscience, and, waiting for fuller revelation, kept within the limits of his own knowledge rather than use a liberty he had not embraced by faith. Theodoret says God attends not to the bare deed but inquires into the design of it. On the clause about not regarding the day the voices divide textually: Gill reports it missing from the Alexandrian copy and the Vulgate but present in most Greek copies, while Ellicott and Robertson judge it no part of the text.
7:
The rule is now grounded in something larger than the dispute. Gill restricts the saying to believers, who do not live to righteous self nor to sinful self nor to the wills of others; Henry says no one who has given up his name to Christ is allowedly a self-seeker, and that the business of our lives is not to please ourselves. Clarke observes that the Greek writers used the phrase of living to oneself for acting according to one's own judgment, and that the Christian must act instead according to the mind of God. Barnes defines the opposite plainly, that to live to ourselves is to make it the great object to become rich or honoured or comfortable, which is the aim of all men but Christians, and adds that where there is a sincere desire to do God's will another motive should be supposed rather than indulgence. Wesley glosses it as being at one's own disposal, doing one's own will. Calvin reasons from the whole to the part: it is no wonder that particular acts should be referred to the Lord's will when life itself ought to be spent wholly to his glory, and it is impiety to undertake anything one is not persuaded will please him. On dying Ellicott notes that even in the act of death the Christian is conscious of his relation to Christ and dies in the Lord, and Robertson that life and death alike focus in the Lord. Theodoret deduces that we are not our own lords, and therefore neither art thou his master nor is he thine, for one Lord we all have.

The ninth verse carries a textual crux and every voice touches it. Gill catalogues the witnesses without deciding: the word revived is omitted by the Vulgate and placed by the Syriac between the dying and the rising, and the Alexandrian copy reads died and lived. Barnes reports the clause and rose as rejected by most modern critics and probably brought into the text from the margin; Clarke adds that Griesbach omits it and that Professor White pronounced the shorter reading indisputably genuine; Ellicott says the best manuscripts substitute simply and lived and calls the Received text a gloss; Robertson reads the verb as an ingressive aorist, he came to life. On the substance Calvin argues that by undergoing death Christ acquired an authority which death cannot destroy, and that by rising he attained a new state of life subject to no change, so that his dominion is eternal. Theodoret calls him the Master of all who destroyed the power of death, and Barnes draws from the previous verse that the soul is not annihilated when a man dies.

The application follows at once. Barnes turns the two charges back on the two parties, the Jewish convert arraigning and the Gentile despising, and says nothing so much prevents either as remembering that both are bought with the same blood and going to the same heaven. Clarke quotes Heylin's saying that the superstitious are prone to judge and those who are not superstitious are prone to despise. Wesley notes that the apostle has turned from the weak brother to the stronger. Calvin argues that to assume the power of judging is to rob Christ of what he alone received from the Father, and that since the Lord has established a fraternal alliance among us an equality ought to be preserved, so that a man taking the judge's bench is a criminal climbing out of the dock. Cyril of Jerusalem, expounding the last judgment, presses that there is no need of allegory here but only to fulfil what is said. On the tribunal itself Ellicott dissents from the rest in a single line, holding that the true reading names the judgment seat of God rather than of Christ.
11:
The proof is drawn from Isaiah, and its force is disputed. Barnes points out that in the prophet the speaker expressly calls himself by the name proper to God alone, and that Paul applies the words to Christ, which he treats as a strong incidental proof that the apostle held the Lord Jesus to be divine, since on no other principle could the quotation have been made. Wesley says as much in a line, that Christ is here termed both Lord and God, and Theodoret that this witness of the prophet proves the completeness of the divinity of the Only-begotten. Calvin will not have the verse used that way: the judgment seat was not doubted among Christians and needed no proof, and the prophet is cited rather to show that all flesh ought to await that judgment with the greatest lowliness, which the bending of the knee expresses. On the second clause Ellicott notes that the Greek will bear either confess or praise, that most commentators prefer the second, and that he is not certain the English version is wrong; Robertson, taking the dative, reads it as giving praise. Gill adds a curiosity of citation, that Justin Martyr quotes a like passage as out of Ezekiel, where no such words stand in the Hebrew or the Septuagint. Barnes and Clarke draw the same practical conclusion from the reckoning that follows, that we shall not answer for one another's conduct but each for his own, and had better see that we can give up our account with joy.

Calvin finds the apostle playing on the word: he forbids us to judge, that is, to condemn, and in the same breath bids us judge, that is, exercise discernment so as not to give offence. Barnes calls this a happy turn of the discussion, since men with an irresistible propensity to pronounce opinions may at least exercise it where it can do no injury, forming a determination about their own conduct instead of a verdict on others, and Robertson calls the verse a wonderfully fine text for modern Christians. Ellicott observes that the second of the two words is the origin of our word scandal and properly means a trap or snare, and that tenderness for the weak is one of the special characteristics of Christianity. Theodoret notes that the rebuke has now turned to the Gentile converts, who would not condescend to the infirmities of the Jews. Henry, drawing the moral of the whole passage, says we must deny ourselves in many cases what we may lawfully do.

The apostle then states his own mind. Chrysostom observes that he does not threaten punishment but simply disburdens the weaker sort of their fears, and that the appeal to the Lord answers the objection that a man's persuasion is no evidence against a law delivered from above; by nature nothing is unclean, but it becomes so by the spirit in which a man uses it, and so becomes unclean to him only and not to all. Theodoret gives the same reason for the phrase, that it forestalled the question who Paul was to legislate against Moses by producing the Lord of Moses himself. Clarke and Wesley take the words as claiming an inspiration or particular revelation, while Ellicott and Robertson read the preposition as in rather than by, a solemn asseveration out of the depths of Christian consciousness and not a conclusion of rational process. Ellicott adds that the uncleanness is thus not an objective property of the thing but a subjective quality in the mind of the man, real for him and to be treated as real; Calvin, agreeing that no meat is impure to a pure conscience, insists that we must regard not only the meats but the brethren before whom we eat.
15:
Ellicott begins with the conjunction, holding the true reading to be for, and traces a connection that leaps over the parenthesis about uncleanness and rejoins the warning against stumblingblocks. He then marks two stages in the verse: to see another do what one's own conscience condemns causes pain, but to be drawn on into doing it oneself is moral ruin. Gill sets out the same gradation at more length, the weak brother grieved, or emboldened to eat and so wounded in conscience, or offended to the point of abandoning his profession. Barnes and Robertson both put the principle as a violation of the law of love, Robertson adding that personal liberty in food is too great a price to pay. Calvin states the second reason as the wasting of the price of Christ's blood, and says we must be basely given up to our own lusts if we prefer meat, a worthless thing, to Christ. Theodoret sharpens the reproach: for him the Lord endured death, while you will not gain life for him by a mere abstinence, but by indulgence contrive his death. Then comes the sharpest division in the chapter. Clarke takes the verse to teach plainly that a man for whom Christ died may perish, and calls the original very emphatic; Wesley says the same in a line. Calvin refuses the inference as negatived by many positive declarations of Scripture, holding that man's inference cannot be right when it contradicts God's word, and that the apostle exhibits the tendency of such conduct without saying it takes effect; but he equally refuses the easy escape, that the destruction meant is only of comfort and edification, for the apostle no doubt meant the ruin of the soul.

What the good is that must not be blasphemed is read three ways. Gill offers either the gospel at large or the doctrine of Christian liberty in particular, and notes that the Vulgate and Syriac read our good rather than yours; Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Wesley all take it of the liberty itself, Barnes reflecting how much strife would have been avoided had Christians observed so plain a rule about dress and rites and ceremonies; Theodoret takes it of faith, and notes that the accusation is made in conjunction with praise, the apostle commending their faith while refusing to let it become a cause of reproach. Clarke turns it into a caution about method: there are many who so manage their good acts as to do little good and a great deal of evil by them, and it requires much prudence to find the proper time even of a good action.

On the kingdom of God the voices agree in substance and differ in reference. Gill takes the phrase of glory, of the principle of grace, and of the gospel church state, none of which consists in anything external; Robertson insists it is not the future kingdom of eschatology but the present reign of God in the heart. Clarke and Wesley expound the three words as pardon and holiness, peace ruling in the soul from a sense of mercy, and a joy that is happiness brought in by the Spirit; Ellicott denies that righteousness and peace here mean imputed righteousness and reconciliation, taking them of the moral condition of the Christian and his concord with his fellows, crowned by a subdued and chastened exultation. Theodoret names concord and zeal as to peace, and love as the spring of joy. Calvin adds the necessary limit: things necessary to build up or preserve the kingdom are by no means to be neglected whatever offence may follow, and only where God's honour is uninjured and religion unhindered is abstaining for love's sake a duty.
18:
The man who serves Christ in righteousness and peace and joy is acceptable to God and approved of men, and the second half of that gives the voices most trouble. Barnes concedes that the wicked world will not love such a life but holds it will commend itself to them as the life men ought to lead; Wesley narrows the word to wise and good men; Calvin narrows it differently, granting that the ungodly often pour out reproaches without cause, defame the innocent with forged calumnies and put a malignant construction on things rightly done, and confining the apostle's meaning to honest judgment blended with no moroseness, hatred or superstition. Clarke notes that it was a common Jewish form of speech that a conscientious observer of the law was pleasing to God and approved of men, and refers to Schoettgen for examples. Ellicott prefers the reading in this way and finds in the phrase the principle of unity holding the sides of the Christian character together. Theodoret draws a different inference altogether: if serving Christ is acceptable to the God of all, then honouring Christ must please him, and to speak evil of Christ or attempt to lower his dignity must offend him.

Gill and Clarke take the exhortation that follows as a plain call to drop the quarrel; Barnes expands it into a rule, that Christians have more things in which they agree than in which they differ, and that where the great common objects are pursued the smaller matters sink into unimportance. Henry warns that many wish for peace and talk loudly for it who do not follow the things that make for peace. Calvin adds the necessary caution that edification is joined to peace precisely because some indulge one another too freely and do much harm by their compliances, so that discretion must decide what may usefully be granted. Ellicott and Robertson both report that the best manuscripts give the indicative here, so then we follow, rather than the exhortation, Ellicott noting that the Received text has good support in the versions and the patristic quotations and that mistakes of this kind were peculiarly liable to be made.

What the work of God is that meat must not destroy is read four ways. Gill offers the righteousness and peace and joy just named, or the weak brother as both creature and new creature, or rather the peace of the church, and insists that a true believer, however weak, cannot himself be destroyed, though the work of peace and edification may be. Barnes takes it of the building God is rearing, and Ellicott of the fabric grace has begun, the gradual formation of a Christian character; Robertson takes it simply of the brother for whom Christ died. Theodoret takes it of faith itself, on the strength of the saying that the work of God is to believe on him whom he has sent. Ellicott and Robertson both observe that the verb is now the opposite of edify, to unbuild or pull down. Calvin, arguing from the three words of the following verse, sets out an ascending scale, the weakened man whose conscience wavers, the stumbling man more gravely perplexed, and the fallen man alienated from religion altogether; Wesley expounds the same three separately. Ellicott, however, reports a remarkable division of authority over the last two clauses, the Sinaitic and Alexandrine against the Vatican and the Graeco-Latin codices with the versions nearly divided, and decides on internal evidence to omit as a gloss the very words on which that scale is built. Clarke, tracing the second word to the stick of a trap, holds it here to mean total apostasy.
22:
The chapter closes on the conscience, and the first question is what is being asked. Ellicott gives up the Received interrogative with some reluctance, in deference to the union of the four best manuscripts, and reads instead that the faith which thou hast, have to thyself before God, reserving the exhibition of it to private communion and not displaying it ostentatiously where it may do harm; Robertson reports the same relative in the old copies. Clarke passes on a third proposal, from Dr. Taylor, that there is no necessity for the interrogative at all and that the two forms of the verb make a doubling, thou hast a right persuasion, now hold it fast. Gill is anxious that the word faith not be stretched: it is not faith in Christ and the doctrines of the gospel, which no man ought to keep in his own breast but should confess before the church, but only a persuasion about things indifferent; and the counsel is not to change that persuasion or cast it away but to hold it within. Calvin turns the same point into a protest. The passage is strangely perverted, he says, by those who conclude from it that it does not matter how devoted a man is to foolish and superstitious ceremonies so long as his conscience is pure before God, for ceremonies belong to worship and are part of our confession, and they who tear faith from confession take from the sun its own heat.

On the beatitude that follows the voices are close together. Barnes makes it a universal proposition, that many men indulge in practices their consciences condemn and many more in practices about which they are in doubt, and that a clear conscience in one's opinions and conduct is the way of peace. Clarke calls it a most excellent maxim by which every part of a man's conduct should be tried, since no man can have peace who sins against his conscience, and warns that a man's passions may allow what his conscience will not. Wesley notes the sharp possibility that a man may allow the thing and yet condemn himself for it. Ellicott renders the clause of the acts a man permits himself, and Robertson quotes the saying of Denney that it is a rare felicity to have a conscience untroubled by scruples, adding that the beatitude cuts both ways. Theodoret finds in the wording an insinuation that the Gentile converts had been in the habit of compelling the Jews to partake of what they shrank from.

The last verse turns on two words. Barnes prefers the margin, he that discerneth and putteth a difference between meats, and Theodoret likewise reads he that maketh a distinction, while the rendering that has passed into the English version is he that doubteth, which Robertson defends as hesitation, the double-mindedness of the epistle of James, and which Calvin describes as a mind vacillating and held suspended by uncertainty. Barnes then enters a caution about the second word: we apply it almost exclusively to future punishment, but it means properly to condemn, and affirms here only that such a man incurs guilt, not that he will inevitably sink to hell; Robertson reads the perfect as standing condemned. On the closing maxim the division is wide. Clarke takes it to reach every work done before the grace of Christ, and cites his own Church's article that such works have the nature of sin; Ellicott denies the extension outright and holds that the principle covers only the case in hand, where conscience is in doubt, and says plainly that Augustine argued wrongly from this passage; Barnes grants the wider proposition is true but denies that it is what is taught here; Wesley and Gill keep it to the man's own persuasion of lawfulness.
